transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-18
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Liu (Redwood SRE advisor), Eva Morales (Hypernova Head of ML Ops), Dr. Samir Patel (Lead Engineer), Lina Park (Platform SRE)

Summary (auto):
Customer seeing repeated KV cache evictions for a small set of 'hot' prefixes which triggers paging to disk and large latency spikes on long-context generative workloads. Discussed hysteresis, prefetch heuristics, TTL tuning, and dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs on VPC/private deployment. Agreed to reproduce in an SE simulation, share telemetry, and run pilot with prefetched hot-prefix set.

Topics: hysteresis, hot-prefix detection, prefetch thresholds, eviction pacing, long-context KV residency, on-prem/VPC I/O implications, quantization tradeoffs for memory pressure.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Monroe: alright hi everyone thanks for making time, um we wanted to get into the specifics of the cache behavior you flagged. is this a good time?
[00:08] Eva Morales: yes totally, thanks Alex. we get these big latency spikes when certain drug-design prompts go long, say 12k plus tokens, and it's like kvcache thrashes and then requests hit disk and everything slows down.
[00:20] Priya Shah: ok can you describe what you mean by thrash, like eviction frequency and are prefixes re-used across sessions or per-user?
[00:27] Dr. Samir Patel: it's mostly a small set of prefixes we call "assay-templates" that are extremely hot; multiple sessions re-use them. but when sequence lengths creep up, we see eviction windows where the same prefix is evicted and immediately re-prefetched, causing spill and high p99.
[00:44] Marcus Liu: just to clarify, are you seeing prefix collisions between unrelated users or the same prefix id reused intentionally?
[00:50] Lina Park: same ID, reused across teams. we tried increasing TTL but that made other prefixes age out faster, so net latency didn't improve.
[00:58] Alex Monroe: ok that signals a locality concentration problem — hot-prefix hotspot. we call this hysteresis when the eviction boundary oscillates. there are a few levers: increase hysteresis window, add a hot-prefix pinlist, or aggressive prefetch + eviction pacing.
[01:12] Eva Morales: whats hysteresis window in practice? like how many tokens or seconds?
[01:17] Priya Shah: good question. hysteresis is the buffer between eviction threshold and re-warm threshold. e.g., if cache size is N, don't evict until you're at N + H, or keep a grace-residency time T after last access. these are tunables.
[01:29] Dr. Samir Patel: we already have a TTL per prefix, but the problem is that prefix size varies widely because of long contexts; some prefixes are 2x larger in token-metadata.
[01:38] Priya Shah: yep that variability complicates eviction heuristics. our runtime uses an LRU with size-aware weights, but when size variance is heavy, weight normalization can still cause churn. you can tune weight vs recency.
[01:50] Lina Park: is there a way to group prefixes? like coalesce related prefixes to avoid partial evictions?
[01:55] Marcus Liu: you can coalesce at application layer by creating a superprefix (concatenate) but that increases memory; runtime-level grouping is possible by marking prefixes with affinity tags so eviction considers groups. that's something we'd need to enable per-customer as a feature flag.
[02:10] [short cross talk, some muffled background noise] Speaker 1: hmm mm hm
[02:18] Alex Monroe: two approaches I want to sketch: one, conservative hysteresis + pinlist for known hot prefixes; two, workload-aware prefetch that prioritizes hot prefixes and staggers re-warm to avoid thundering herd.
[02:30] Eva Morales: the pinlist sounds promising. but we need to ensure we don't starve other prefixes, we've got thousands of low-frequency prefixes.
[02:38] Priya Shah: you can do a hybrid: reserve R% of KV capacity for pinned prefixes and leave the rest LRU for opportunistic entries. our telemetry dashboard can show you how many prefixes would fit if we reserve 15% vs 30%.
[02:50] Dr. Samir Patel: how do we determine hotness? access count, reuse within window…? we saw a pattern where some prefixes spike for 10 minutes then go quiet.
[02:59] Priya Shah: hotness signals are usually a combination: access count per minute, reuse across sessions, and prefix byte-size. we prefer a decay function: a weighted moving average with half-life so short bursts don't permanently pin.
[03:12] Lina Park: what about prefetch heuristics for long-context? when a session grows beyond X tokens, should we prefetch the next K prefixes?
[03:19] Marcus Liu: prefetching ahead by predicted next-prefix IDs works if your model prompts are deterministic. for generative stochastic outputs it's trickier. a safe heuristic: when sequence length crosses threshold S, prefetch likely continuation prefixes for pinned set only. avoids over-prefetching.
[03:33] [00:03:35] Alex Monroe: i wanna pause and ask about paging — you said hit disk, is that local NVMe or network NFS?
[03:40] Lina Park: currently network-attached NVMe on our private cluster, with mixed I/O latency depending on contention — sometimes 5ms, sometimes 40ms.
[03:48] Priya Shah: that variance is the killer. on-host NVMe or dedicated intra-node memory store avoids that variability. for VPC/private deployments we strongly recommend co-locating KV hotstores on the same instance as the serving runtime if you need sub-10ms tail latency.
[03:59] Eva Morales: we are on an on-prem cluster and have restrictions on adding hardware. so software mitigations are more realistic short-term.
[04:06] Alex Monroe: understood. software-side, prefetched pinlist + hysteresis + eviction pacing will reduce disk pressure. also backoff on parallel prefetches — don't prefetch everything at once.
[04:16] Dr. Samir Patel: what about compression/quantization of KV values to reduce footprint? we already quantize weights but not the KV store.
[04:24] Priya Shah: quantizing KV entries (float -> int8 or int16) can reduce memory but increases CPU cost on decode and may affect generation quality slightly if KV stores positional embeddings. it's a tradeoff; we can run per-prefix quality checks. often 4-bit/8-bit encodings for ephemeral KV are acceptable.
[04:40] Lina Park: do you support on-the-fly dequantization in the runtime without major latency penalty?
[04:44] Marcus Liu: yes we have optimized paths for int8 dequantization using vectorized kernels, but when CPU is saturated you'll see added tail latency. this is why co-scheduling and isolating CPU for dequantization is important.
[04:56] [05:00] Alex Monroe: another technique is staged eviction: when the cache is under pressure, evict coldest small entries first and delay evicting large but hot entries to avoid re-warm cost. size-aware staging reduces excessive I/O.
[05:13] Eva Morales: that sounds promising — can we see a simulation?
[05:17] Priya Shah: yes I'll generate a synthetic workload that mirrors your prefix distribution and run both staging and hysteresis configs. i'll include latency/p99/p999 and IO ops/sec.
[05:26] Dr. Samir Patel: i want to mention we saw a specific spike tied to a nightly batch that pre-populates contexts; maybe that is clobbering cache at 02:00.
[05:34] Lina Park: yes we run a scheduled retrain that hits many prefixes in a short window; it's a write-heavy pattern.
[05:39] Priya Shah: write-heavy jobs can evict hot entries unexpectedly. you might schedule background writes to a lower-priority window or use write-throttling. also consider marking training prefixes with low priority so they don't evict production pinned prefixes.
[05:50] Alex Monroe: quick note: we can expose priority tags on prefixes so platform can avoid eviction of high-priority keys during batch windows.
[05:57] [06:00] Eva Morales: ok can we talk about deployment options — hosted vs dedicated vs private? if we go with Redwood Dedicated or Private, what changes?
[06:08] Alex Monroe: for Dedicated we provide reserved GPU pools and can dedicate local NVMe hotstores with higher SLOs. Private (VPC/on-prem) can be configured to co-locate KV on GPU nodes; but you'll manage physical storage. both allow us to push kernel optimizations and tuning.
[06:21] Dr. Samir Patel: are there security implications with pinlists or affinity tags? we need audit logs and RBAC.
[06:27] Priya Shah: yes we log pinlist changes and have RBAC around feature flags. we can add audit entries to your SIEM. Redwood Private also supports KMS integration for at-rest encryption of KV payloads.
[06:38] Lina Park: what's the operational burden to run our own co-located NVMe? we have constrained ops headcount.
[06:44] Marcus Liu: there's additional Ops — monitoring, disk health, compaction. but we provide runbooks and optional managed ops for Dedicated customers. for Private installs we supply automation scripts for deployment and upgrades.
[06:56] [06:57] Alex Monroe: ok time check — about 10 minutes left. i want to summarize the agreed playbook and next steps.
[07:04] Eva Morales: yep please.
[07:06] Alex Monroe: action items: SE (Priya) will produce a synthetic workload and run prefetched/hysteresis/staging configs and send results; Hypernova (Lina) will share 7-day eviction telemetry and note the nightly batch windows; Alex will send security checklist and pricing for pilot. we also proposed reserving 15% KV capacity for pinned prefixes while experimenting.
[07:24] Dr. Samir Patel: can you include a sample config? like the exact flags to turn on staging/hysteresis in the runtime?
[07:30] Priya Shah: yes i'll include a sample config and a helm snippet for the private deploy. i'll also include a script that generates hot-prefix pinlist based on top-k accesses.
[07:40] Lina Park: for the pilot timeline, we want to try config changes in staging this week and a controlled pilot next week.
[07:46] Alex Monroe: sounds good — we'll aim to have SE results by Monday 1/25 and a follow-up the week of 1/31.
[07:53] [08:00] Eva Morales: quick question on metrics — what telemetry should we export? eviction count, evicted-bytes, prefix-size-distribution, access-rate, IO-latency?
[08:10] Priya Shah: exactly. eviction_count, eviction_reason (TTL/size/pressure), prefix_size_bytes histogram, access_rate_per_prefix, prefetch_attempts, prefetch_success_rate, disk_io_latency p50/p90/p99. we'll give you a grafana export template.
[08:23] Dr. Samir Patel: reasonable. also can we add model-level correlation: map requests to model version so we can see if a rollout changed patterns.
[08:31] Marcus Liu: yes correlate request headers; we recommend tagging requests with model_version and route_id.
[08:36] [08:40] Alex Monroe: ok wrapping up, quick risk callouts: quantization reduces memory but raises CPU load, pinned capacity reduces available opportunistic cache, prefetch increases writes/IO. we'll show the tradeoffs in the sim.
[08:52] Eva Morales: great, thanks everyone.
[08:54] Alex Monroe: thanks all, we'll follow up with deck and config snippets. talk soon.

Recap (auto):
- Root cause: hot-prefix concentration + variable prefix sizes causing eviction oscillations and disk paging during long-context workloads.
- Short-term mitigations: pinlist reservation (~15%), hysteresis window tuning, staged eviction, prefetch backoff, schedule-sensitive write-throttling.
- Medium-term: co-locate NVMe with serving runtime for lower tail-latency or move to Dedicated plan with guaranteed local hotstore; consider KV quantization with per-prefix QA.

References mentioned:
- "runbook: kvcache-hysteresis-config.yaml" (will be attached by Priya)
- Telemetry template & grafana dashboard (link to shared drive)
- Pilot pricing spreadsheet (Alex to send)

End of meeting.
